label: Opus 5.5 · Grok Bot
title: An overnight motion design studio
lines: You go to bed with an idea. You wake up to a finished, reviewed, sixty-frames-per-second motion graphic.
No After Effects. No timeline. Five bots on one cloud computer, working the night shift.
This is how to build that studio on Grok Bot, using Claude Opus 5.5, and the parts most tutorials skip.

label: The one-prompt era
title: Everyone stops at the same place
lines: In September, one prompt template for a code-only UI animation pulled 1.2 million views and twenty-one thousand saves.
Thousands of people tried it. Most of them got one great clip, and a laptop that sat there rendering all night.
That's a demo. A studio is different: someone plans, someone builds, someone renders, someone judges, and someone ships.

label: The plan
title: Five bots. One night. One finished film.
lines: So here's the plan: five bots, each with one job, handing work to each other while you sleep.

label: Why Grok Bot
title: You don't pick the model
lines: On October seventh, Elon Musk posted that Grok Bot would use the best back end model for any given task, including Claude Opus 5.5.
Simple questions route to small, fast models. Hard ones route to large models. And routing to Opus doesn't change what you pay per token.

label: The catch
title: No model picker. No effort dial.
lines: Here's the catch. Grok Bot has no model picker, and you can't even see which model handled a request.
The viral one-shot clips were made in Claude Code on the highest effort settings. You don't get that dial here.

label: The fix
title: Replace the dial with structure
lines: So you don't chase a magic prompt. You replace the missing dial with structure:
a written spec, gates between stages, and a critic that never wrote the code it's grading.

label: The machine
title: One computer, shared by every bot
lines: Every bot on your account shares one persistent cloud computer: the same files, the same browser logins, the same terminal.
Each bot gets its own screen, so they can work in parallel. And closing your laptop doesn't stop any of it.

label: What survives
title: Files survive. Installs don't.
lines: But read the fine print. Files in slash workspace and your logins survive updates and recovery.
Installed packages, apps and background services don't. The computer also sleeps when it's idle, and can update itself before it does.

label: Design for it
title: No daemons. Everything restartable.
lines: That shapes everything. No long-running daemons. A bootstrap script that reinstalls ffmpeg, Python and a headless browser in one command.
And every render has to be resumable, so a nap in the middle of the night costs minutes, not the whole job.

label: No GPU
title: Why code beats a 3D renderer here
lines: Users report about eight CPU cores, sixteen gigs of RAM, and no GPU.
So you animate with HTML, CSS and SVG, and leave Blender out of the default path. The bottleneck isn't the model. It's capturing frames.

label: House style
title: Rules every bot shares
lines: Next, write the studio's rules down once, as a skill. Private skills are one library shared by all your bots.
The house style says: every frame is a pure function of time, fonts load from files, and something new appears every two to four seconds.

label: The banned list
title: Ban defaults by name
lines: Then a banned list: centered titles on gradients, everything fading in at once, particle bursts, bouncy easing, dead air.
Anthropic's own guidance warns that even when you tell the model to avoid generic choices, it tends to swap one default for another.
So you ban each cliché by name, and every time a new one sneaks in, the Critic adds a line.

label: The roster
title: Five bots, one job each
lines: Now the roster. The Director turns your request into a brief and a storyboard, and owns it all the way to delivery.
The Animator writes the film as code. The Render bot is the only one allowed to render.
The Critic scores, and never writes code. And Delivery hands you the finished file.

label: Why split it
title: One renderer. Separate judge.
lines: Why only one renderer? They share one machine. Two renders at once means both crawl, and both might get cut off by sleep.
Why a separate critic? Because anyone grading their own work goes easy on it. Models included.

label: State
title: The folder is the state machine
lines: Bots forget. Chats scroll away. Files don't. So every project is a folder, and every file is a state:
brief, beats, storyboard approved, code ready, final passed, delivered.
If the computer gets rebuilt, or a bot loses its context, one look at the folder tells you exactly where each project stands.

label: The engine
title: Start from a proven template
lines: For the engine, start from that open template. Its build rules are the whole trick.
Springs are closed-form, so a value that changes target many times is just a sum of springs, still a pure function of time.
And the last line matters most: show the state list on the beat grid before you write any code.

label: Storyboard gate
title: Approve the plan, then build
lines: That list is your storyboard. Fixing a line costs one message. Fixing a finished scene costs a rewrite. So nothing gets built until you approve it.

label: Rendering
title: Every frame, drawn on demand
lines: Rendering never plays the animation in real time. A script asks the page for any moment, seek t, screenshots it, and moves on.
Frames land on disk as numbered files. That folder is the progress bar, so a restart simply picks up at the first missing frame.

label: Motion blur
title: Four moments, one frame
lines: For motion blur, capture four moments inside each frame and let ffmpeg blend them. It's the same idea as a camera shutter staying open.
With no GPU, slow frames just take longer. Nothing drops, because nothing is real time.

label: The numbers
title: What it costs on two cores
lines: On a two-core Linux box with no GPU, a fifteen-second test rendered as a draft in forty-eight seconds.
The final, at sixty frames with motion blur, took about six minutes. Before any full render, the template renders one still per beat to catch problems early.

label: Beat grid
title: Every change lands on a beat
lines: Use a properly licensed track. A Python script measures the beat grid, and every scene change snaps to it.
It also writes a click track, so you can check the sync by ear in five seconds instead of squinting at waveforms.

label: The Critic
title: A critic that can't watch video
lines: The Critic can't watch an MP4, so the Render bot turns the film into images:
a thirty-frame contact sheet, fifteen frames at phone width, and the first and last frames side by side.

label: The rubric
title: Six scores. Eight or better.
lines: It scores six things: the hook in the first two seconds, readability on a phone, motion, variety, composition and brand.
Everything has to reach eight. If not, only the three worst problems go back to the Animator, so fixes stay focused.
Three failed rounds, and the studio stops and asks you, instead of burning your usage at three in the morning.

label: The night shift
title: Routines run the clock
lines: Routines run the clock. At nine P M, the Director picks up new requests. Through the night, Render works the queue.
At eight A M, Delivery sends you what passed. You approve storyboards before bed, and wake up to finished films.

label: Routine rules
title: Small print that matters
lines: A few details matter. Schedules follow the time zone in settings. A new routine waits for its next slot, and Test does real work.
And every run spends usage, so an hourly check costs twenty-four runs a day whether there's work or not.

label: Failure modes
title: What breaks, and the fix
lines: Plan for what breaks. Usage runs out: keep checks cheap and cap rounds. The computer sleeps mid-render: resume from the frames on disk.
Routines get paused after a long stretch away: check in once a day. And copy every finished film out of the computer, because a rebuild should never cost you a delivery.

label: Tonight
title: Start with one film
lines: To start tonight: write the house style skill, create the five bots, add the bootstrap script, and run one fifteen-second test end to end.
Only when one film survives the whole pipeline, turn on the routines.

label: The point
title: From one prompt to a studio
lines: The viral clips proved a model can make one beautiful video. The studio is how you make the next hundred, while you sleep.
